blocks.text: Experiments on the masses of nuclei show that the mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of the protons and neutrons that make it up. The missing mass is the mass defect: dm = [Z mp + (A - Z) mn] - m_nucleus (19.1), where mp is the mass of a proton, mn the mass of a neutron and m_nucleus the mass of the whole nucleus. The missing mass has been converted into energy in forming the nucleus, given by Einstein's mass-energy relation: dE = (dm) c^2 (19.2). This energy is the binding energy (B.E.) of the nucleus.

blocks.title: Binding energy
blocks.text: The binding energy of a nucleus is the work that must be done on the nucleus to break it into its constituent neutrons and protons. A better measure of stability is the binding energy per nucleon, the average energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons.

Binding energy can be regarded as negative, like gravitational potential energy taken as zero at infinity. Masses of sub-atomic particles are usually given in atomic mass units (u): 1 u is one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12, 1 u = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg (1.66 x 10^-24 g). Some atomic masses in u: e 0.00055, n 1.008665, 1H 1.007276, 2H 2.014102, 3H 3.01605, 3He 3.01603, 4He 4.002603, 7Li 7.016004, 10Be 10.013534, 14N 14.0031 and 17O 16.9991.

Find the mass defect and binding energy of the helium nucleus, given mp = 1.672623 x 10^-27 kg, mn = 1.674929 x 10^-27 kg and m_nucleus = 6.646786 x 10^-27 kg. Solution: dm = 2 mp + 2 mn - m_nucleus = 2(1.672623) x 10^-27 + 2(1.674929) x 10^-27 - 6.646786 x 10^-27 = 6.695104 x 10^-27 - 6.646786 x 10^-27 = 0.048318 x 10^-27 kg. B.E. = dm c^2 = 0.048318 x 10^-27 kg x (3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1)^2 = 4.34862 x 10^-12 J. In electron volts, B.E. = 4.34862 x 10^-12 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.7 x 10^7 eV = 27 MeV, about 6.8 MeV per nucleon.

A graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A (Fig 19.1) shows how stable a nucleus is and whether energy can be obtained from it by fission or fusion. The hydrogen nucleus, with just one proton, has zero binding energy. The rise from hydrogen to helium is large, which suggests a large energy release when hydrogen is converted into helium. The curve reaches a maximum of about 8.7 MeV per nucleon for iron, 56-26-Fe, the most stable nuclide; the region of most stable nuclei is between A = 50 and 80. After that the binding energy per nucleon decreases steadily to the end of the curve.

So the binding energy per nucleon is less for very light and very heavy nuclei. If a heavy nucleus splits into two nuclei that lie near the top of the curve, their nucleons are more tightly bound: this is nuclear fission, already used to produce huge amounts of power. Similarly, if two light nuclei combine into a single nucleus, as when deuterium and tritium fuse into a more stable helium nucleus, a huge amount of energy is released: this is fusion. It is hard to start and needs extremely high temperatures, as in the Sun and other stars. In general, energy is obtained from any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases.

blocks.alt: A graph of binding energy per nucleon (0 to 9 MeV) against nucleon number A (0 to 250). Points for H (0), 2H, Li, 4He and C rise steeply; the red curve reaches a broad maximum near Fe (about 8.8 MeV), passes Ag and falls slowly to U (about 7.6 MeV). A green arrow labelled fusion goes up from light nuclei towards the peak; a purple arrow labelled fission goes from U towards the middle of the curve.
blocks.caption: Binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number (original graph after Fig 19.1).
blocks.long_description: Nuclei near iron are the most tightly bound. Moving towards the peak from either side, by splitting heavy nuclei or joining light ones, increases the binding energy per nucleon and so releases energy.
